title: Maximum Product Subarray — track running max AND min (negatives flip).
shortTitle: Maximum Product Subarray — Track Running Max AND Min
topicTitle: Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — running sum, reset w

s1_definition.profdef: The Maximum Product Subarray problem finds the contiguous slice of an array whose element product is largest. Because multiplying by a negative number flips the sign, a very small, most negative, running product can become the largest once multiplied by another negative. The solution keeps both a running maximum product and a running minimum product ending at each position, swapping them when the current element is negative, and updates a global best. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India tracks Rajesh's daily growth factors for a portfolio, numbers above one for a gain day and below one or negative for a loss day, and an analyst wants the consecutive stretch whose multiplied effect is largest. The twist is that a run of two bad, negative, days multiplied together becomes positive and possibly huge, so you must remember not only the best running product but also the worst, because today's worst could become tomorrow's best after a sign flip.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep running max and min products, swap them on a negative element, and track the global best.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Maximum Product Subarray problem finds the contiguous slice of an array whose element product is largest. Because multiplying by a negative number flips the sign, a very small, most negative, running product can become the largest once multiplied by another negative. The solution keeps both a running maximum product and a running minimum product ending at each position, swapping them when the current element is negative, and updates a global best. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India tracks Rajesh's daily growth factors for a portfolio, numbers above one for a gain day and below one or negative for a loss day, and an analyst wants the consecutive stretch whose multiplied effect is largest. The twist is that a run of two bad, negative, days multiplied together becomes positive and possibly huge, so you must remember not only the best running product but also the worst, because today's worst could become tomorrow's best after a sign flip.

**One line to remember:** Keep running max and min products, swap them on a negative element, and track the global best.

sections.s2_technical:
The additive Maximum Subarray needs only a running maximum because adding never flips order. Multiplication is different: a single negative element turns the largest product into the smallest and the smallest into the largest. So keeping only a running maximum is not enough, because the most negative running product is a hidden candidate that becomes the winner the moment it is multiplied by another negative.

You keep three values: a running maxProduct, a running minProduct, both the best and worst products of a subarray ending at the current position, and a global best. All start at the first element. For each remaining element you first notice that if the element is negative, the roles of max and min will flip, so you swap maxProduct and minProduct before updating. Then you set maxProduct to the maximum of the element alone and the element times the previous maxProduct, and minProduct to the minimum of the element alone and the element times the previous minProduct. Finally you update the global best with maxProduct.

The swap-on-negative step is the heart of it. A negative element multiplied by the previous maxProduct gives a small, possibly most negative, number, while the same negative multiplied by the previous minProduct, which may itself be negative, gives a large positive number. By swapping before the max and min updates, the large positive candidate correctly flows into maxProduct and the small negative into minProduct.

A senior point is handling zeros. A zero resets both running products because any product through a zero is zero. Taking the maximum of the element alone, which is zero, and the element times a previous product, which is also zero, naturally restarts the run at the next element. So zeros are handled without special code, as long as you include the element-alone option in both max and min updates.

Another senior point is money and precision. If the values are exact growth factors I use BigDecimal with multiply, max, and min via compareTo, avoiding floating-point drift that would compound dangerously over a long multiplied chain. I guard the empty array by rejecting it, and a single element array returns that element.

A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal maxP=f[0],minP=f[0],best=f[0]; for(int i=1;i<n;i++){ if(f[i].signum()<0){ var t=maxP; maxP=minP; minP=t; } maxP=f[i].max(maxP.multiply(f[i])); minP=f[i].min(minP.multiply(f[i])); best=best.max(maxP); }` returns the largest contiguous product exactly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores Rajesh's daily portfolio growth factors, where a value above one means a gain and a negative value means a reversal, and a feature finds the consecutive stretch of days whose multiplied compound effect is the largest, to highlight his strongest compounding run. The feature must scan long histories fast. Finding the maximum product subarray is exactly this.

This is exactly how Maximum Product Subarray works in Java — tracking both the running best and running worst product because a negative day flips which one is winning.

Problem 2 — Reversal days are negative, so two reversals in a row compound into a large positive, and some days are flat zero which must reset the run, and all factors are exact BigDecimal to avoid compounding drift. This shows the sign-flip handling, the zero reset, and money precision.

What the code will do: a `MaxProductAnalyzer` with `bestContiguousProduct(BigDecimal[] factors)` keeping running max and min with swap-on-negative, tracking the best in BigDecimal. The demo finds Rajesh's strongest compounding stretch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the growth factors are `2, 3, -2, 4`.

Step 1: maxProduct, minProduct, and best all start at the first factor `2`.

Step 2: at factor `3`, which is positive so no swap, maxProduct becomes the maximum of `3` alone and `2 * 3 = 6`, which is `6`, and minProduct becomes the minimum of `3` and `6`, which is `3`. Best improves to `6`.

Step 3: at factor `-2`, which is negative, we first swap so maxProduct is `3` and minProduct is `6`. Then maxProduct becomes the maximum of `-2` and `3 * -2 = -6`, which is `-2`, and minProduct becomes the minimum of `-2` and `6 * -2 = -12`, which is `-12`. Best stays `6`. Notice the worst running product is now a large negative `-12`, which is being carried deliberately.

Step 4: at factor `4`, positive so no swap, maxProduct becomes the maximum of `4` and `-2 * 4 = -8`, which is `4`, and minProduct becomes the minimum of `4` and `-12 * 4 = -48`, which is `-48`. Best stays `6`.

Step 5: the loop ends with best `6`, the product of the slice `2, 3`, found in a single linear pass. The flip demo `-2, 0, -1` resets at the zero and the best achievable contiguous product is `0`, since no two negatives are adjacent without a zero between them.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z INFO Best product = 6
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z INFO Best compounding product for Rajesh = 6
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z INFO Best product = 0
2026-10-26T18:40:00Z INFO Flip case best = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [2,3,-2,4]  maxP=2 minP=2 best=2
    │
    ▼
  each factor f: if f<0 swap(maxP,minP); maxP=max(f,maxP*f); minP=min(f,minP*f)
    │ f=3   maxP=6  minP=3   best=6
    │ f=-2  swap→maxP=3,minP=6 ; maxP=-2 minP=-12
    │ f=4   maxP=4  minP=-48  best=6
    ▼
  best = 6  (slice [2,3])
    ▼
  Output: strongest compounding stretch
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Product Subarray finds the contiguous slice whose element product is largest, and the twist over the additive version is that multiplying by a negative number flips the sign, so the most negative running product is a hidden candidate that can become the winner after another negative. I solve it in a single linear pass with constant space by carrying both a running maximum product and a running minimum product ending at each position, plus a global best.

The key step is swapping the running max and min whenever the current element is negative, before I update them. A negative times the old maximum gives a small, often most negative, number, while the same negative times the old minimum gives a large positive, so the swap routes the large positive into the max and the small negative into the min. That is why keeping only a running max, which works for the additive problem, silently fails here.

I also handle zeros and precision cleanly. A zero naturally resets both running products because taking the maximum and minimum against the element alone, which is zero, restarts the run at the next element, so no special case is needed. For money I use BigDecimal with multiply, max, and min, which avoids the floating-point drift that would compound dangerously over a long multiplied chain, and I reject an empty array up front.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on Rajesh's daily portfolio growth factors, where reversal days are negative, to find the consecutive stretch whose compound multiplied effect was strongest, correctly rewarding runs where two reversals flipped into a large gain. Explaining the dual max-min state, the swap-on-negative, and the zero reset shows the interviewer that I understand why multiplication needs a fundamentally different state than addition.
